title: Effects of Indoor Lighting, Gender, and Age on Mood and Cognitive Performance

findings.antecedent: Warm white lighting (3000K, ~3000Kelvin) vs. cool white lighting (4000K, ~4000Kelvin)
findings.consequent: Change in positive mood in younger adults (age ~23 years)
findings.statement: Younger adults best preserved positive mood in warm (reddish) white lighting while working with cognitive tasks for 90 minutes
findings.quote: younger females preserved (had the least decrease in) the positive mood better than the younger males did
theory_links: affective source theory - lighting conveys emotional meanings

findings.antecedent: Warm white lighting (3000K) vs. cool white lighting (4000K)
findings.consequent: Change in positive mood in older adults (age ~65 years)
findings.statement: Older adults preserved positive mood better in cool (bluish) white lighting, opposite effect to younger adults
findings.quote: for the older adults (about 65 years old), cool (more bluish) white lighting accounted for the identical effect
theory_links: age-differentiated emotional appraisal of light color

findings.consequent: Negative mood change across lighting conditions
findings.statement: Females preserved negative mood better than males (smallest increase was .78 vs. 2.25)
findings.quote: A main effect of gender, F(1, 72) = 4.48, p < .05, showed that females preserved the negative mood better than did males (smallest increase was .78 vs. 2.25)
findings.mechanism: females more emotionally reactive to affective sources

findings.antecedent: Type of lamp (warm vs. cool) and age interaction
findings.statement: Older adults preserved negative mood better in cool white lighting; younger showed opposite effect in warm white lighting
findings.quote: A two-way interaction between type of lamp and age, F(1, 72) = 7.64, p < .01, revealed that the older adults preserved (had the smallest increase in) the negative mood better in the cool white lighting than did the younger adults

findings.statement: Younger adults performed significantly better on problem-solving than older adults (18.2 vs. 6.1 out of 32)
findings.quote: The younger performed significantly better than the older adults (younger = 18.2 vs. older = 6.1 out of 32)
findings.mechanism: age-related decline in visual and cognitive processing

findings.antecedent: Gender and age interaction on problem-solving
findings.statement: Younger females performed better than younger males; no significant effect in older adults
findings.quote: The younger females were also shown to perform better than the younger males, t(38) = 2.0, p < .05, and a nonsignificant tendency toward the contrary effect among the older females and males was indicated

findings.statement: Younger participants performed significantly better on long-term recall than older participants (10.2 vs. 6.5 out of 18.0)
findings.quote: A main effect of age, F(1, 72) = 15.46, p < .001, showed that the younger participants performed significantly better than the older (younger = 10.2 vs. older = 6.5 out of 18.0)

findings.statement: Younger adults performed significantly better on long-term recognition than older adults (9.7 vs. 8.9 out of 18)
findings.quote: The same effect as above was obtained. The younger adults performed significantly better than the older, F(1, 72) = 5.79, p < .05 (younger = 9.7 vs. older = 8.9 out of 18)

findings.antecedent: Age and gender on short-term recall
findings.statement: Younger participants performed significantly better than older on short-term recall (younger = 6.5 vs. older = 4.6 out of 16); females performed better than males
instruments_used: Free recall of colored word lists
findings.quote: the younger participants performed significantly better than their older colleagues, F(1, 72) = 52.08, p < .001 (younger = 6.5 vs. older = 4.6 out of 16). Women performed significantly better (6 vs. 5) than men, F(1, 72) = 13.36, p < .001

scope_conditions.task: free recall of 3 word lists, 16 words each

findings.antecedent: Word list valence (positive vs. negative) and mood
findings.statement: Participants recalled significantly more positive than negative words, indicating mood-congruent memory effect
findings.quote: The participants recalled significantly (F(2, 144) = 6.01, p < .01) more positive than negative words, t(79) = 3.36, p < .001

findings.statement: Younger adults assessed room light as brighter than older adults (3.4 vs. 2.8 on 5-point scale)
findings.quote: A main effect of age on the bright dimension, F(1, 72) = 5.36, p < .05, showed that the younger adults assessed the room light as brighter than did the older participants (3.4 vs. 2.8 on a scale ranging from 1 to 5)

findings.antecedent: Type of lamp (cool vs. warm) across ages
findings.statement: Regardless of lamp type, younger adults perceived room light as cooler than older adults (2.8 vs. 2.1 on scale)
findings.quote: The same effects were revealed on the cool dimension, F(1, 72) = 5.46, p < .05. Regardless of the type of lamp, the younger participants assessed the room light as cooler than their older colleagues did (2.8 vs. 2.1 on a scale ranging from 1 to 5)

findings.antecedent: Interaction: lamp color (warm vs. cool) and gender on mood
findings.consequent: Cognitive performance in memory and problem-solving
findings.statement: Type of lamp that induced least negative mood and preserved positive mood best in each gender also enhanced cognitive performance in long-term memory and problem-solving tasks
findings.quote: two-way interactions between type of lamp and gender on positive and negative mood and cognitive performance showed that the type of lamp that induced the least negative mood and preserved the positive mood best in each gender also enhanced the cognitive performance in long-term memory and problem-solving tasks

limitations: Sample recruited from college students and pensioners' clubs, may not represent general population
Short-term exposure (90 minutes) may not reflect long-term effects of lighting
Gender-related words were evenly distributed in recall task, potentially limiting mood-congruence effects
Only two lighting conditions tested (cool and warm); additional color temperatures would strengthen findings
No baseline or control condition without lighting manipulation
Age groups were artificially separated (young ~23, old ~65); continuous age analysis not provided
overall_theory_links: environmental_psychology - physical environment affects mood and cognition
affective_source_theory - lighting conveys different emotional meanings to different demographic groups
mood_congruence_in_memory - positive mood enhances recall of positive information
cognitive_aging_theory - age-related declines in processing speed and memory
gender_differences_in_emotion - females more sensitive to affective sources in environment
color_psychology - warm vs cool color temperature affects emotional appraisal differently across age groups
